## Synthesis: research report

**Question:** Tablet and desktop application interface design as disciplines distinct from responsive web design. Narrow scope. TABLET: (1) why a stretched phone layout fails on a tablet and what the named alternatives are — Apple's NavigationSplitView and three-column layouts, Material's canonical layouts (list-detail, supporting pane, feed) and the navigation rail, and the window size class systems both platforms use (Apple size classes, Material window size classes with their breakpoint values in dp); (2) iPadOS multitasking — Split View, Slide Over, Stage Manager, and what a designer must guarantee when the app does not own the full screen; (3) hybrid input — designing for touch and pointer and an external keyboard simultaneously, including iPadOS pointer effects and hover states that must not be load-bearing; (4) the specific numeric breakpoints and layout guidance each platform publishes for large screens, and Google's stated large-screen app quality guidelines. DESKTOP: (5) desktop application design conventions that browser-based design does not cover — menu bar and application menus, window management and resizing behavior, multi-window and document-based apps, keyboard shortcut conventions and where they differ between macOS and Windows, right-click context menus, and drag and drop between windows; (6) what Apple's macOS Human Interface Guidelines and Microsoft's Windows design guidance (Fluent) each require that a web design would omit; (7) Electron and Tauri desktop apps specifically — the named failure of shipping a website in a window, and what a designer must add to make a web-technology app feel native (platform keyboard conventions, window chrome, menu integration, offline behavior). Prioritize primary sources: developer.apple.com Human Interface Guidelines for iPadOS and macOS, m3.material.io adaptive layout guidance, developer.android.com large screen guidelines, and learn.microsoft.com Windows design docs. Reject blog restatements where a primary source exists.

21 claims survived 3-vote adversarial verification. Merge semantic duplicates and synthesize.

## Confirmed claims
### [0] Apple's iPadOS HIG requires apps to adapt to multitasking modes as a first-class appearance change, alongside orientation, Dark Mode, and Dynamic Type — i.e. an iPad app must not assume it owns a fixed full-screen canvas, and must also survive transition to running under macOS.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/platforms/designing-for-ipados/ (primary)
Quote: "Adapt seamlessly to appearance changes — like device orientation, multitasking modes, Dark Mode, and Dynamic Type — and transition effortlessly to running in macOS, letting people choose the configurations that work best for them."
Verifier evidence (high): VERBATIM MATCH CONFIRMED ON LIVE PRIMARY SOURCE (fetched 2026-08-01). WebFetch on the HTML page returned nothing (Apple HIG is a JS-rendered SPA), so I pulled Apple's own DocC JSON backing the page: https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/platforms/designing-for-ipados.json (HTTP 200, 22,224 bytes, metadata.title = "Designing for iPadOS"). Extracted text contains the quoted sentence character-for-character: "Adapt seamlessly to appearance changes — like device orientation, multitasking modes, Dark Mode, and Dynamic Type — and transition effortlessly to running in macOS, letting people choose the configurations that work best for them."

1. Quote supports claim. All three claim elements are literal: (a) "multitasking modes" is listed inline in the same enumeration as orientation/Dark Mode/Dynamic Type, so "first-class appearance change alongside" is not an interpolation; (b) "must not assume a fixed full-screen canvas" is a fair restatement, not an overreach — the same page independently says "Learn best practices for designing a responsive layout for resizable app windows" and "People frequently have multiple apps open at the same time, and they appreciate viewing more than one app onscreen at once"; (c) "transition to running under macOS" is Apple's own phrase "transition effortlessly to running in macOS".

2. Contradicting evidence: none found. The only counter-angle I could construct is the modal verb — the HIG frames this list with "To help your experience feel at home in iPadOS, prioritize the following ways...", i.e. guidance, not an App Review rule. But "requires" survives even that, because the technical layer now hard-enforces it: UIRequiresFullScreen is deprecated and per Apple's own TN3192 ("Migrating your iPad app from the deprecated UIRequiresFullScreen key", developer.apple.com/documentation/technotes/tn3192) apps can no longer opt out of iPad multitasking and dynamic resizing; iPadOS 26 betas warn "UIRequiresFullScreen will soon be ignored, and support for all orientations will soon be required," and UIScene life cycle becomes mandatory in the release after iOS 26 (WWDC25 session 282, "Make your UIKit app more flexible"). So the HIG's soft "prioritize" is backed by a hard platform requirement.

3. Source quality: primary, Apple's own documentation endpoint, exact URL cited in the claim. Matches claim strength.

4. Not outdated. Deliberately checked the iPadOS 26 multitasking overhaul (Split View and Slide Over removed June 2025 in favor of a Mac-like windowing model; Stage Manager retained). The fetched page is the post-overhaul version — it references resizable app windows, window controls, the menu bar, the new pointer and updated effects, and Liquid Glass — and it still uses the generic phrase "multitasking modes". Because the claim says "multitasking modes" and never names Split View or Slide Over, the iPadOS 26 change does not date it. CAVEAT FOR DOWNSTREAM USE: any derived write-up that expands "multitasking modes" into "Split View, Slide Over, Stage Manager" IS outdated for iPadOS 26+ — Slide Over and classic Split View are gone; the current model is windowing + tiling + optional Stage Manager.

5. Not marketing/forum/benchmark material — it is design guidance on the vendor's normative spec page.

### [1] Apple states that iPad users combine multiple simultaneous input modes — Multi-Touch gestures, virtual keyboards, an attached physical keyboard or pointing device, Apple Pencil, and voice — so hybrid input is the documented default assumption on iPadOS, not an edge case.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/platforms/designing-for-ipados/ (primary)
Quote: "Inputs. People can interact with iPad using Multi-Touch gestures and virtual keyboards, an attached keyboard or pointing device, Apple Pencil, or voice, and they often combine multiple input modes."
Verifier evidence (high): Verified against the live primary source, not a blog restatement. Fetched Apple's own documentation JSON backing the HIG page (https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ipados.json, HTTP 200, metadata title "Designing for iPadOS"; the claimed URL https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/platforms/designing-for-ipados/ resolves 200 to the same article). The "Inputs" bullet reads verbatim, with inline links resolved: "Inputs. People can interact with iPad using Multi-Touch gestures and virtual keyboards, an attached keyboard or pointing device, Apple Pencil, or voice, and they often combine multiple input modes." So the supporting quote is exact, word for word, including "they often combine multiple input modes."

Context strengthens rather than weakens the claim. The bullet sits under the page's opening framing: "start by understanding the following fundamental device characteristics and patterns that distinguish the iPadOS experience" — i.e. inputs are listed as a fundamental characteristic that must inform design decisions, alongside Display, Ergonomics, App interactions, System features. The same page's best-practice list then says: "Use viewing distance and input mode to help you determine the size and density of the onscreen content you display" and "Let people use Multi-Touch gestures, a physical keyboard or trackpad, or Apple Pencil, and consider supporting unique interactions that combine multiple input modes." Two independent statements on the same primary page, one descriptive and one prescriptive.

Currency: the page is current, not a stale snapshot — it references Liquid Glass, the menu bar, window controls, and "resizable app windows," i.e. the iPadOS 26-era HIG, fetched 2026-08-01.

Counter-evidence search turned up nothing disputing it; a WebSearch for the phrase returned only secondary blog restatements (netguru, bitcot, brilworks, Medium) that agree, plus an unrelated Microsoft UWP multi-input page. No credible source contradicts or qualifies it.

One honest caveat, not enough to refute: the claim's phrasing "documented default assumption ... not an edge case" is a mild interpretive gloss on Apple's "often combine" and "consider supporting." Apple asserts frequency and lists inputs as fundamental; it does not literally use the words "default assumption." The gloss is defensible — "often" plus placement among fundamental characteristics is the opposite of edge-case framing — but a strict reading would want the claim to say "Apple documents multi-mode input as a fundamental iPad characteristic that people often combine" rather than importing "default assumption." Substance is sound; only the rhetorical temperature is slightly above the source.

### [2] Apple's stated large-display guidance for iPad is to minimize modal interfaces and full-screen transitions — the opposite of the phone-derived pattern of pushing full-screen views — and to place controls within reach but out of the way.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/platforms/designing-for-ipados/ (primary)
Quote: "Take advantage of the large display to elevate the content people care about, minimizing modal interfaces and full-screen transitions, and positioning onscreen controls where they’re easy to reach, but not in the way."
Verifier evidence (high): VERBATIM MATCH CONFIRMED ON PRIMARY SOURCE (fetched live 2026-08-01). I bypassed the JS-rendered HTML (WebFetch returned only the page title) and pulled Apple's own documentation JSON: https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ipados.json. Under the heading "Best practices" the first bullet reads exactly: "Take advantage of the large display to elevate the content people care about, minimizing modal interfaces and full-screen transitions, and positioning onscreen controls where they're easy to reach, but not in the way." Both halves of the claim map 1:1 onto Apple's sentence — "minimize modal interfaces and full-screen transitions" and "place controls within reach but out of the way" ("easy to reach, but not in the way"). The claim's characterization as "large-display guidance" is accurate because Apple's own sentence opens with "Take advantage of the large display."

CROSS-CHECK FOR THE IMPLIED CONTRAST: I pulled the sibling page designing-for-ios.json. Its "Best practices" list contains no equivalent line — it says instead "Help people concentrate on primary tasks and content by limiting the number of onscreen controls..." and "it tends to be easier and more comfortable for people to reach a control when it's located in the middle or bottom area of the display." So the minimize-modality/minimize-full-screen-transition instruction is genuinely iPad-specific in Apple's own structure, which supports (structurally, not verbally) the claim's contrast with phone patterns.

ONE QUALIFICATION, not sufficient to refute: the em-dash aside "the opposite of the phone-derived pattern of pushing full-screen views" is the claim author's gloss, NOT Apple's wording. Apple never frames it as an inversion of an iPhone pattern; the word "opposite" is interpolation. It should be presented as the author's reading, not as Apple's statement. Additionally, "minimize" is not "prohibit" — Apple's separate HIG pages (Modality, Going full screen) still endorse full-screen modal style for immersive content and multistep tasks, so the guidance is a bias, not a ban. Neither point contradicts the substance.

NOT OUTDATED: text was retrieved from the live Apple endpoint today, post-iPadOS 26 windowing changes. NOT MARKETING/BLOG: first-party Apple HIG, the exact primary source the research question demanded. Searches surfaced only blog restatements (nadcab.com, brilworks.com, medium) — no credible source disputes or qualifies the guidance.

### [3] Apple's current iPadOS layout guidance frames multitasking as macOS-style free window resizing rather than the older fixed Split View / Slide Over modes: windows resize continuously down to a minimum width and height, and designers must account for the full range of possible window sizes. Notably, the page never names Split View, Slide Over, or Stage Manager anywhere in its iPadOS section.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout (primary)
Quote: "People can freely resize windows down to a minimum width and height, similar to window behavior in macOS. It’s important to account for this resizing behavior and the full range of possible window sizes when designing your layout."
Verifier evidence (high): Verified against the primary source's own data payload (developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout.json — the rendered HTML page is JS-only, which is why plain WebFetch returns just the title).

QUOTE: exact verbatim match. The "Platform considerations > iPadOS" section reads: "People can freely resize windows down to a minimum width and height, similar to window behavior in macOS. It's important to account for this resizing behavior and the full range of possible window sizes when designing your layout. For guidance, see Multitasking and Windows."

NEGATIVE CLAIM: holds. String counts over the ENTIRE page payload (body text, references, topic sections, metadata — not just the iPadOS section): "Split View" = 0, "Slide Over" = 0, "Stage Manager" = 0.

CORROBORATION BEYOND ONE PAGE: I also pulled the two pages the iPadOS section links to. multitasking.json and windows.json each contain 0 occurrences of all three terms. Apple's Multitasking page now reads only "On iPad, people can view and interact with the windows of several different apps at the same time." So this is a systematic HIG vocabulary shift to window language, not a single-page omission — which makes the claim stronger, not weaker.

CURRENCY: page metadata alert-date = 2025-09-09, supported-platforms = ios,ipados,macos,tvos,visionos,watchos; content matches the iPadOS 26 windowing model. Not outdated. Primary source, not a blog restatement, not marketing.

SUPPORTING iPadOS-SECTION TEXT (also verified verbatim): "Design for a full-screen view first, and only switch to a compact view when a version of the full layout no longer fits... prefer hiding tertiary columns such as inspectors as the view narrows." and "Window controls provide the option to arrange windows to fill halves, thirds, and quadrants of the screen, so it's important to check your layout at each of these sizes on a variety of devices."

ONE CAVEAT (not fatal): the phrase "rather than the older fixed Split View / Slide Over modes" is the claimant's inference from absence plus Apple's macOS analogy — Apple never writes an explicit contrastive "rather than." Also, the iPadOS section DOES link to a Multitasking page, so it would be wrong to extend this into "Apple dropped multitasking guidance"; what was dropped is the legacy mode nomenclature. The claim as written stays within what the source supports.

Local artifacts: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-taha/a37ae9f9-eb70-4000-aa63-8f4f998a4172/scratchpad/layout.json, multi.json, win.json, layout.txt

### [4] Apple prescribes a specific collapse order for adaptive layouts: design the full-screen layout first, defer switching to a compact view as long as possible, and for multi-column layouts hide tertiary columns (such as inspectors) before collapsing further.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout (primary)
Quote: "As someone resizes a window, defer switching to a compact view for as long as possible. Design for a full-screen view first, and only switch to a compact view when a version of the full layout no longer fits. This helps the UI feel more stable and familiar in as many situations as possible. For more complex layouts such as [split views], prefer hiding tertiary columns such as inspectors as the view narrows."
Verifier evidence (high): VERBATIM MATCH CONFIRMED at the cited primary source. developer.apple.com's Layout HIG page renders via JS (plain WebFetch returned an empty body), so I fetched the backing documentation JSON: https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout.json (HTTP 200, 116 KB, fetched 2026-08-01). Extracted text contains, contiguously and word-for-word: "As someone resizes a window, defer switching to a compact view for as long as possible. Design for a full-screen view first, and only switch to a compact view when a version of the full layout no longer fits. This helps the UI feel more stable and familiar in as many situations as possible. For more complex layouts such as split views, prefer hiding tertiary columns such as inspectors as the view narrows. Test your layout at common system-provided sizes, and provide smooth transitions."

Checklist results:
(1) SUPPORTED, not an overreach. All three components of the claim map onto explicit sentences: "design the full-screen layout first" = "Design for a full-screen view first"; "defer switching to a compact view as long as possible" = verbatim; "hide tertiary columns (such as inspectors) before collapsing further" = "prefer hiding tertiary columns such as inspectors as the view narrows," read alongside the preceding "defer switching to a compact view for as long as possible." The claim's "before collapsing further" is a light interpolation but is entailed by the two adjacent sentences.
(2) NO CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE FOUND. WebSearch for the exact phrases surfaced no source disputing it; this is a claim about what Apple publishes, which is directly verifiable rather than contestable. Adjacent HIG pages are consistent, e.g. Split views: "Prefer using a split view in a regular — not a compact — environment... A split view can display a tertiary pane if items in the secondary pane contain additional content."
(3) SOURCE QUALITY ADEQUATE. Primary vendor documentation, exactly matching the strength of the claim (a design-guidance claim, not an empirical one).
(4) CURRENT, NOT OUTDATED. The same page section references iPadOS free window resizing "similar to window behavior in macOS," window controls tiling to "halves, thirds, and quadrants," and elsewhere the Liquid Glass material — i.e. the iPadOS 26-era HIG, current as of fetch date.
(5) NOT MARKETING/FORUM. First-party design guidance, no benchmark or press-release framing.

TWO QUALIFICATIONS worth carrying into the writeup, neither sufficient to refute:
(a) SCOPE: this passage lives under "Platform considerations > iPadOS" (structural extraction of the JSON confirms the H3 heading), not under the platform-neutral "Adaptability" section. The claim's unqualified "Apple prescribes... for adaptive layouts" should be stated as iPadOS guidance; the macOS subsection of the same page contains no equivalent collapse-order text.
(b) MODALITY: Apple's wording is "prefer" / "defer... for as long as possible" — recommendation, not requirement. "Prescribes" is marginally stronger than the source's register; "recommends" would be exact.

Local extraction saved at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-taha/a37ae9f9-eb70-4000-aa63-8f4f998a4172/scratchpad/layout.json

### [5] Apple names the concrete iPad window sizes a designer must test against — halves, thirds, and quadrants of the screen produced by the system window controls — rather than publishing CSS-style pixel breakpoints.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout (primary)
Quote: "Test your layout at common system-provided sizes, and provide smooth transitions. Window controls provide the option to arrange windows to fill halves, thirds, and quadrants of the screen, so it’s important to check your layout at each of these sizes on a variety of devices. Be sure to minimize unexpected UI changes as people adjust down to the minimum and up to the maximum window size."
Verifier evidence (high): Verified via the primary source's underlying JSON data (developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout.json, fetched directly since the rendered HTML is a JS shell). The supporting quote matches verbatim: 'Test your layout at common system-provided sizes, and provide smooth transitions. Window controls provide the option to arrange windows to fill halves, thirds, and quadrants of the screen, so it's important to check your layout at each of these sizes on a variety of devices.' Positionally, this text (byte offset 19566) sits directly under the page's 'iPadOS' H3 heading (offset 17857) and before the 'macOS' heading (offset 20899), confirming it is iPad-window-size guidance as claimed, immediately preceded by an iPadOS paragraph noting 'People can freely resize windows down to a minimum width and height, similar to window behavior in macOS.' Searching the full page text for the literal word 'breakpoint' returns zero matches — Apple never uses breakpoint terminology here. The page does list numeric pt values elsewhere (e.g. '320 pt' unfocused content width, device screen dimensions in pixels, size classes) but these are grid-column specs and device reference tables, not window-resize breakpoints tied to layout switching — reinforcing rather than contradicting the claim's 'rather than CSS-style pixel breakpoints' framing. Cross-checked the companion 'Multitasking' HIG page (developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/multitasking) via the same JSON-data technique: also zero matches for 'breakpoint' and no explicit pt-based window-size thresholds published. The only minor overreach is describing halves/thirds/quadrants as 'concrete... window sizes' — they are named categories, not literal pixel/pt dimensions — but this is a defensible paraphrase given the quote instructs designers to test at exactly these named sizes, not a misrepresentation.

### [6] Apple's size class system is binary (regular or compact) per axis, not a numeric breakpoint ladder; the accompanying specification table lists every iPad model — Pro 12.9-inch, Pro 11-inch, Pro 10.5-inch, Air 13-inch, Air 11-inch, iPad 11-inch, iPad 9.7-inch, iPad mini 7.9-inch — as 'Regular width, regular height' in BOTH portrait and landscape, whereas iPhones vary by orientation (e.g. iPhone 17 Pro Max: compact width/regular height portrait, regular width/compact height landscape).
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout (primary)
Quote: "A size class is a value that’s either regular or compact, where regular refers to a larger screen or a screen in landscape orientation and compact refers to a smaller screen or a screen in portrait orientation. […] Different size class combinations apply to the full-screen experience on different devices, based on screen size."
Verifier evidence (high): Directly fetched Apple's live DocC JSON payload backing https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout (retrieved via https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout.json, the JSON data source that renders the cited HTML page). The section titled "iOS, iPadOS device size classes" contains the exact prose: "A size class is a value that's either regular or compact, where [regular] refers to a larger screen or a screen in landscape orientation and [compact] refers to a smaller screen or a screen in portrait orientation... Different size class combinations apply to the full-screen experience on different devices, based on screen size" — matching the claim's supporting quote verbatim (bracketed terms render as inline glossary-reference links in the raw JSON, which explains the quote's blank spots). The accompanying table (49 rows, extracted in full) confirms every specific detail in the claim: all eight named iPad models — iPad Pro 12.9-inch, Pro 11-inch, Pro 10.5-inch, Air 13-inch, Air 11-inch, iPad 11-inch, iPad 9.7-inch, iPad mini 7.9-inch — are each listed as "Regular width, regular height" in BOTH the Portrait orientation and Landscape orientation columns, exactly as claimed. The iPhone rows confirm orientation-dependent size classes, and the specific example cited (iPhone 17 Pro Max) is verbatim in the table: "Compact width, regular height" (portrait) / "Regular width, compact height" (landscape). No part of the claim is an overreach or misread — it is a direct, accurate restatement of primary-source table data, not an inference from prose. Source is the highest-quality primary source available (Apple's own current live documentation), and content is current (table includes iPhone 17 lineup, consistent with an Aug 2026 access date).

### [7] Apple's HIG explicitly instructs designers to prefer split views in a regular (not compact) horizontal size class environment, because a compact environment — iPhone in portrait is the named example — cannot display multiple panes without wrapping or truncating content. This is Apple's primary-source statement of why a phone-width layout and a multi-pane tablet layout are different design problems, keyed to size classes.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/split-views (primary)
Quote: "**Prefer using a split view in a regular — not a compact — environment.** A split view needs horizontal space in which to display multiple panes. In a compact environment, such as iPhone in portrait orientation, it's difficult to display multiple panes without wrapping or truncating the content, making it less legible and harder to interact with."
Verifier evidence (high): The supporting quote was verified verbatim via independent web searches that surfaced the exact phrasing from Apple's own HIG Split Views page: "Prefer using a split view in a regular — not a compact — environment. A split view needs horizontal space in which to display multiple panes. In a compact environment, such as iPhone in portrait orientation, it's difficult to display multiple panes without wrapping or truncating the content, making it less legible and harder to interact with." This is a primary source (developer.apple.com HIG), directly on-topic, and current guidance still live as of the search (no deprecation/redirect notice, page resolves under both the short URL and the fuller components/layout-and-organization path). The claim's equating of "regular/compact" with "horizontal size class" is independently corroborated by Apple's own Adaptivity and Layout HIG page, which states "There are two size classes that can apply to the horizontal dimension: regular... and compact..." — so the claim's framing is Apple's own established terminology, not an invented link. iPhone-in-portrait is indeed the explicit named example of a compact environment. The claim's core assertions (prefer split views in regular not compact; iPhone portrait as the compact example; difficulty with multi-pane display without wrapping/truncating) are all directly supported. No search turned up any dispute, deprecation, or contradicting guidance. Minor stylistic tightening ("difficult" → "cannot...without") is within normal paraphrase tolerance and doesn't change the substance.

### [8] On iPadOS, Apple's split view supports either two vertical panes (Mail) or three vertical panes (Keynote), and the named implementations are SwiftUI's NavigationSplitView and UIKit's UISplitViewController. This confirms the two-column and three-column split-view pattern as Apple's canonical large-screen layout, with the specific API names.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/split-views (primary)
Quote: "In iPadOS, a split view can include either two vertical panes, like Mail, or three vertical panes, like Keynote."
Verifier evidence (high): The quote is verified accurate: both a WebSearch snippet directly from developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/split-views and an independent scraped mirror (raw.githubusercontent.com/tmaasen/apple-dev-mcp .../split-views.md) return the identical sentence, "In iPadOS, a split view can include either two vertical panes, like Mail, or three vertical panes, like Keynote." The mirror also shows the same HIG page immediately follows that sentence with "For developer guidance, see Navigation Split View and UISplit View Controller" — confirming the claim's added detail that SwiftUI's NavigationSplitView and UIKit's UISplitViewController are the named implementations is not fabricated but taken from the same source page, directly adjacent to the quoted text. The claim's synthesis ("confirms the two-column and three-column split-view pattern as Apple's canonical large-screen layout, with the specific API names") is a fair, non-overreaching restatement — it does not claim split view is the *only* canonical pattern, just that this is a named, documented one, which matches the source. Source is a current, primary Apple HIG page (NavigationSplitView, referenced, shipped iOS 16/2022, still current as of Aug 2026; UISplitViewController is long-standing and still Apple's documented API). No contradicting evidence found.

### [9] Apple requires iPadOS split-view layouts to be designed for narrow, compact, and intermediate window widths — not just full screen — because iPad windows are fluidly resizable, and requires that navigating between panes remain logical at every width. This is the primary-source obligation a designer must meet when the app does not own the full screen (multitasking / resizable windows).
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/split-views (primary)
Quote: "**Account for narrow, compact, and intermediate window widths.** Since iPad windows are fluidly resizable, it's important to consider the design of a split view layout at multiple widths. In particular, ensure that it's possible to navigate between the various panes in a logical way."
Verifier evidence (high): Verified the quote independently via two separate fetch paths: (1) r.jina.ai proxy of the live developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/split-views page, and (2) a GitHub-hosted mirror (tmaasen/apple-dev-mcp) of the same HIG content. Both return the identical verbatim text under the page's iPadOS platform-considerations section: "Account for narrow, compact, and intermediate window widths. Since iPad windows are fluidly resizable, it's important to consider the design of a split view layout at multiple widths. In particular, ensure that it's possible to navigate between the various panes in a logical way." This exactly matches the claim's supporting quote and its placement (iPad-specific split-view guidance). The claim's paraphrase ("not just full screen," "requires... at every width") is a fair, non-overreaching restatement of the directive imperative language Apple uses ("Account for," "ensure that"). Checked for a contradicting/outdating signal: iPadOS 26 (current as of Aug 2026) reportedly retired the OS-level multitasking features named "Split View" and "Slide Over" in favor of freely resizable "Windowed Apps," but that is a different concept from the HIG "Split Views" *component/layout pattern* (list-detail navigation) the claim and source actually address — and if anything, freely resizable windowing reinforces rather than undermines the claim that iPad app windows are fluidly resizable and app UI must adapt across widths. The live-fetched quote confirms this guidance is still current content on Apple's site today, not a stale/superseded snippet. No credible source was found disputing or qualifying this specific HIG guidance.

### [10] Apple's iPadOS pointer system defines exactly three named content effects — highlight, lift, and hover — each with a prescribed use case: highlight for small elements with a transparent background, lift for small elements with an opaque background, and hover for large elements with customizable scale, tint, and shadow. The system applies highlight by default to bar buttons, tab bars, segmented controls, and edit menus, and lift by default to app icons and Control Center buttons.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pointing-devices (primary)
Quote: "iPadOS defines three content effects that bring focus to different types of interactive elements in your app: highlight, lift, and hover. […] By default, iPadOS applies the highlight effect to bar buttons, tab bars, segmented controls, and edit menus. […] By default, iPadOS applies the lift effect to app icons and to buttons in Control Center. […] Use highlight for a small element that has a transparent background. Use lift for a small element that has an opaque background. Use hover for large elements and customize the scale, tint, and shadow attributes as needed"
Verifier evidence (high): Independently fetched developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pointing-devices (via r.jina.ai reader since direct WebFetch returned only the JS-shell title). Retrieved text confirms every element of the claim verbatim: "iPadOS defines three content effects that bring focus to different types of interactive elements in your app: highlight, lift, and hover." Usage guidance: "Use highlight for a small element that has a transparent background." / "Use lift for a small element that has an opaque background." / "Use hover for large elements and customize the scale, tint, and shadow attributes as needed." explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.
